label: L6
title: Transformers from Scratch I: Training a Transformer Model, End-to-End
brief: Lecture 6 swaps the function class for a Transformer while keeping the cross-entropy loss and gradient-descent solver unchanged. The running task is ATIS slot filling (English to SQL): a 123-way BIO classification for every token, so the output is as long as the input. Tokens become vectors through a learned nn.Embedding table, after integer IDs and one-hot are rejected. Self-attention makes each token's vector a weighted average of all tokens' vectors, with weights given by a softmax of dot products; in this lecture the layer has no trainable parameters (Lecture 7 adds Q, K, V). Multi-head attention, a per-token feed-forward layer and added position vectors complete the Transformer encoder, which stacks because input and output have the same shape. A one-layer SlotTagger (334,075 parameters) reaches 0.961 token accuracy against a 0.602 always-O baseline.
kp: Three ingredients: the function class changes to a Transformer; the cross-entropy loss and gradient-descent solver stay the same.
Slot filling (ATIS, English to SQL) is sequence labelling: one of 123 BIO slot labels per token, so the output is as long as the input.
Integer IDs invite meaningless arithmetic (denver − boston = 1). One-hot is honest but carries no similarity and is V cells long.
nn.Embedding(V, d) is a learned V×d table. Looking up a row equals multiplying the table by a one-hot vector (a bias-free Linear layer).
Requirements: output as long as the input (comes free), use the surrounding context, use word order.
Self-attention: each contextual vector is a weighted average of all tokens' vectors, with weights = softmax of dot products.
This lecture's attention has no trainable parameters. Lecture 7 adds Q, K and V, residual connections and layer norm.
Multi-head: run several attentions in parallel, concatenate per token, then a Dense layer maps back to d. Then the same MLP, Linear(d, 4d) → ReLU → Linear(4d, d), runs on each token.
Attention is order-blind (the scramble test). The fix is to add a position vector (fixed sine waves or learned) to each token's embedding.
Embedding + position → multi-head attention → feed-forward is the Transformer encoder. Same shape in and out, so blocks stack (GPT-3 has 96).

topics.x: Turning 'find me flights from BOS to LGA' into SQL needs to know which words fill which fields. Every token gets one of 123 BIO labels (B- opens a field, I- continues it, O is outside), so this is a per-token 123-way classification rather than one label per sentence.

Integer IDs let the model do arithmetic it has no right to do. One-hot vectors fix that but make every word equally far from every other and are as long as the vocabulary. A learned nn.Embedding(V, d) table, which is a bias-free Linear layer applied to one-hots and trained by gradient descent, places words used alike close together.

A token's contextual vector is $\sum_j w_{ij} x_j$, with weights that are non-negative and sum to one. The weights come from relatedness: dot products of the vectors, pushed through a softmax so they become a proper average. Applied to every token at once this gives six vectors in and six out, using no new parameters.

topics.n: Multi-head attention and the feed-forward layer
topics.x: Several attention computations run in parallel, each meant to capture its own notion of 'related'. Their outputs are concatenated per token and projected back to d by one Dense layer. Each token's vector then passes on its own through the same MLP, Linear(d, h) → ReLU → Linear(h, d), with h = 4d in the original paper.

topics.n: Positional encoding and the Transformer encoder
topics.x: A weighted average ignores order, so 'the train left the station' and 'the station left the train' give identical contextual vectors. Adding a position-dependent vector to each token embedding fixes this. Embedding + position → multi-head attention → feed-forward is the Transformer encoder (Vaswani et al., 2017), and it stacks because input and output shapes match.

SlotTagger adds token and learned position embeddings, runs one nn.TransformerEncoderLayer, and applies Linear(d, 123) to give per-token scores, transposed to the shape cross_entropy expects. The training loop is unchanged apart from building the model. It reaches 0.961 token accuracy against a 0.602 always-O baseline, and its attention weights link boston to from and denver to to.

cards.f: What kind of task is ATIS slot filling?
cards.b: Sequence labelling: one label per token, so the output is as long as the input. Most tokens are O (outside any field).
cards.x: It is not sentence classification, where one label covers the whole input.

cards.f: BIO tags: what do B-, I- and O mean?
cards.b: B- opens a field, I- continues it, and O means the token is outside any field. Example: boston → B-fromloc.city_name.
cards.x: A two-word city takes B- on the first word and I- on the second.

cards.f: How many classes does the slot tagger predict, and how often?
cards.b: 123 slot types, so it runs a 123-way classification once per token.
cards.x: Cross-entropy runs over 123 classes per token instead of 10 per image.

cards.f: Why not feed words to the model as integer IDs (boston = 12, denver = 13)?
cards.b: The model can add and subtract the IDs and would treat denver − boston = 1 as meaningful. Nothing it finds there is true.
cards.x: One-hot removes the false arithmetic but brings costs of its own.

cards.f: What are the two costs of one-hot encoding?
cards.b: (1) No word is closer to any other: boston is as far from denver as from Tuesday. (2) Each vector is as long as the vocabulary, tens of thousands of cells that are almost all zero.
cards.x: It encodes identity only, not meaning.

cards.b: A learned table with V rows of length d, one per token. Looking up row i equals multiplying the table by token i's one-hot vector, so it is a Linear layer with no bias. The rows start random and are trained by gradient descent.
cards.x: Nobody tells it what boston means. Words used alike end up close together.

cards.f: What three requirements must the sequence architecture meet?
cards.b: (1) Output as long as the input. (2) Use the surrounding context. (3) Use word order.
cards.x: Requirement 1 comes free: build the layer to emit one vector per input token.

cards.f: How is token i's contextual vector computed?
cards.b: $\hat{x}_i = \sum_j w_{ij} x_j$: a weighted average of all tokens' stand-alone vectors, with $w_{ij} \ge 0$ and $\sum_j w_{ij} = 1$.
cards.x: 'The whole of attention is choosing the w's.'

cards.f: Where do the attention weights come from in Lecture 6?
cards.b: From relatedness: take the dot products $x_i \cdot x_j$ and apply a softmax over j, so the weights are positive and sum to one.
cards.x: Raw dot products can be negative and do not sum to 1, so they cannot be used directly as weights.

cards.f: How many trainable parameters does Lecture 6's self-attention layer have?
cards.b: None. Every weight comes from the embeddings through dot products and a softmax, which is plain arithmetic.
cards.x: Lecture 7 gives the layer something to learn: the Q, K and V matrices.

cards.f: How does multi-head attention combine its heads?
cards.b: Each head returns a vector per token. The vectors are concatenated (e.g. 3 heads × 4 = 12 numbers) and one Dense layer maps them back to d (12 → 4).
cards.x: The size never changes: six vectors in, six vectors out.

cards.f: What is the feed-forward layer in a Transformer block?
cards.b: Linear(d, h) → ReLU → Linear(h, d), with h = 4d in the original paper. It runs on each token's vector separately, using the same weights for every token.
cards.x: Six boxes in the picture, but one MLP in the code.

cards.f: Why does the encoder need positional encoding, and how is it added?
cards.b: A weighted average does not care about order, so scrambled sentences give identical vectors token for token. The fix is to add a vector that depends only on position to each token's embedding.
cards.x: The original paper uses fixed sine waves; position vectors can also be learned.

cards.f: What does the Lecture 6 encoder leave out, and what does Lecture 7 add?
cards.b: (1) Attention has nothing to learn → Q, K, V. (2) Deep stacks lose the signal → residual connections. (3) Vectors drift in scale → layer normalisation.
cards.x: These are the faint 'Add & norm' boxes in the standard diagram.

cards.b: emb(x) + pos(positions) → nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d, heads, 4d) → nn.Linear(d, 123), giving scores per token, then .transpose(1, 2) for cross_entropy.
cards.x: Only the model line changes in the training loop.

cards.f: How well does the slot tagger do?
cards.b: 334,075 parameters and 0.961 token accuracy (357 wrong out of 9,198), against 0.602 for always predicting O.
cards.x: Most tokens are O, so always quote the majority-class baseline.

quiz.q: Turning 'i want to fly from boston at 7 am' into database fields is framed in Lecture 6 as which kind of task?
o: Sequence labelling: one label per token, so the output is as long as the input
Sentence classification: one label for the whole query
Sequence generation: emit a SQL string token by token
Unsupervised clustering of tokens into 123 groups
quiz.e: Every token gets a slot, most of them O, so the output has the same length as the input. Sentence classification is tempting, but it would give one label for the whole query and could not say which word is the departure city.

quiz.q: In the BIO scheme, what does the tag B-fromloc.city_name on 'boston' mean?
o: boston opens a fromloc.city_name field
boston continues a field opened by the previous token
boston is outside any field
boston closes the fromloc.city_name field
quiz.e: B- opens a field, I- continues it, and O is outside. 'Continues' describes I-, not B-.

quiz.q: Using BIO tags, how should 'new' and 'york' be tagged in 'i want to fly from new york'?
o: B-fromloc.city_name, I-fromloc.city_name
B-fromloc.city_name, B-fromloc.city_name
I-fromloc.city_name, I-fromloc.city_name
O, B-fromloc.city_name
quiz.e: The first word opens the field (B-) and the second continues it (I-). Tagging both B- would mark two separate one-word cities, and I-fromloc.city_name is in the label set for exactly this case.

quiz.q: Why does Lecture 6 reject feeding words in as integer IDs (boston = 12, denver = 13)?
o: The model can do arithmetic on the IDs and read meaning into differences such as denver − boston = 1
Integer IDs make every input vector as long as the vocabulary
GPUs cannot process integer inputs
Integer IDs cannot be converted to one-hot vectors
quiz.e: Numbers can be added and subtracted, and the model would find false structure in them. Vectors as long as the vocabulary are a cost of one-hot encoding, not of integer IDs.

quiz.q: Vocabulary V = 10,000 and embedding size d = 128. How many learned parameters does nn.Embedding(V, d) have?
quiz.e: The table has V rows of d numbers: 10,000 × 128 = 1,280,000. Lookup is a Linear layer with no bias, so adding 128 bias terms (1,280,128) is wrong.

quiz.q: In Lecture 6's self-attention, what is token i's contextual vector?
o: A weighted average of all tokens' stand-alone vectors, with weights that sum to one
Token i's stand-alone vector, unchanged
The plain sum of all tokens' vectors, each with weight 1
The concatenation of all tokens' vectors
quiz.e: It is $\sum_j w_{ij} x_j$ with weights that sum to one, so the result is an average with the same size as each input. A plain sum is not an average, and concatenation would change the size.

quiz.q: station = (0.60, 0.80) and the = (0.94, −0.33). What is station · the?
quiz.e: 0.60 × 0.94 + 0.80 × (−0.33) = 0.564 − 0.264 = 0.30, which is low, so the words are not related. Dropping the minus sign gives 0.83, and 0.96 is station · train.

quiz.q: Why can't raw dot products be used directly as attention weights?
o: They can be negative and need not sum to one, so the result would not be an average
They are too expensive to compute for long sentences
They lie between 0 and 1 but do not add up to 1
They ignore the angle between the vectors
quiz.e: A weight of −0.4 is not an amount of attention, and without summing to 1 the average is not an average. The softmax fixes both. Dot products are not confined to [0, 1], and for unit vectors they measure exactly the angle.

quiz.q: Token i has dot-product scores ($\ln 2$, 0, 0) with three tokens whose vectors are (1, 0), (0, 1) and (0, 0). Using softmax weights, what is its contextual vector?
quiz.e: The softmax gives (2, 1, 1)/4 = (0.5, 0.25, 0.25), so the vector is 0.5·(1, 0) + 0.25·(0, 1) + 0.25·(0, 0) = (0.50, 0.25). Using the raw scores as weights gives (0.69, 0), and taking only the top-scoring token gives (1, 0).

quiz.q: How many trainable parameters does the self-attention layer built in Lecture 6 have?
o: None: the weights come from the embeddings through dot products and a softmax
One d×d query matrix
One learned weight for every pair of tokens
V×d, shared with the embedding table
quiz.e: 'There is nothing here to train … just arithmetic.' Query, key and value matrices only arrive in Lecture 7, so choosing the query matrix mixes the two lectures up.

quiz.q: Three attention heads each return 4 numbers per token. What does the Dense layer after concatenation map?
o: 12 numbers in, 4 out
4 numbers in, 12 out
12 numbers in, 12 out
4 numbers in, 4 out, after averaging the heads
quiz.e: Concatenation gives 3 × 4 = 12 numbers per token, and one Dense layer brings the token's vector back to 4, where it started. Keeping 12 would make each layer grow the vectors, and the heads are concatenated, not averaged.

quiz.q: In Lecture 6's parameter-free attention, what is the catch with running three heads in parallel?
o: With no parameters of their own, the heads compute identical outputs; they only become distinguishable once each gets its own parameters
Each head sees only a third of the tokens
Concatenating the heads permanently triples the vector size
Someone must assign each head a pattern, e.g. verbs to subjects
quiz.e: The slide notes that heads only become distinguishable once they have their own parameters (Lecture 7). Every head sees all the tokens, the Dense layer restores the size, and patterns such as verb–subject emerge from training rather than being assigned.

quiz.q: With d = 128 and hidden width h = 4d, how many weight-matrix entries (ignoring biases) does one feed-forward layer Linear(d, h) → ReLU → Linear(h, d) have?
quiz.e: h = 512, and the two matrices have 128×512 + 512×128 = 131,072 entries. Counting only one Linear gives 65,536, and using h = d gives 32,768. The count does not grow with sentence length because the same MLP is applied to every token.

quiz.q: Without positional information, what does self-attention give for 'the train left the station' versus 'the station left the train'?
o: Identical contextual vectors, token for token
Different vectors, because reordering changes the dot products
Vectors that differ only for 'left'
A shape error, because the order changed
quiz.e: A weighted average does not care about the order of its terms, so each word gets the same vector in both sentences. That is a property of the average, not a bug. Dot products depend only on the vector pairs, not on their positions.

quiz.q: 'sat' has token vector (1.20, 5.30) and position vector (0.91, −0.42). What enters the attention layer?
quiz.e: The two vectors are added element by element: (1.20 + 0.91, 5.30 − 0.42) = (2.11, 4.88). Subtracting, multiplying element by element, or concatenating are not what the encoder does, and concatenating would change the size.

quiz.q: SlotTagger defines self.pos = nn.Embedding(MAXLEN, d) and computes self.emb(x) + self.pos(arange(L)). Which statement is correct?
o: Positions are learned vectors, one row per position, added to the token embeddings, unlike the fixed sine waves of the original paper
Positions use the fixed sine waves of the original paper
Positions are concatenated with the token embeddings, doubling d
Positions are handled by the padding mask inside the encoder
quiz.e: An nn.Embedding table is trained by gradient descent, so these position vectors are learned. The slides say the original paper's sine waves 'can equally be learned'. The '+' means addition, not concatenation, and the padding mask only hides padding tokens.

quiz.q: Going from the Fashion-MNIST classifier to SlotTagger, what changes in the training loop?
o: Only the line that builds the model; optimizer, loader, loss and backward pass are unchanged
Cross-entropy is replaced by a sequence-specific loss
Adam is replaced by plain SGD
The backward pass through attention has to be written by hand
quiz.e: The slide marks every other line '# unchanged'. cross_entropy now runs over 123 classes per token, made possible by transpose(1, 2). Autograd still handles loss.backward().

quiz.q: SlotTagger gets 357 tokens wrong out of 9,198, and always predicting O scores 0.602. Which conclusion is right?
o: Accuracy ≈ 0.961, which removes about 90% of the baseline's errors
Accuracy ≈ 0.039, worse than the baseline
Accuracy ≈ 0.961, which removes about 60% of the baseline's errors
Accuracy ≈ 0.961, which is impressive without any baseline because it is above 0.9
quiz.e: 1 − 357/9198 ≈ 0.961. The error rate falls from 0.398 to 0.039, a cut of about 90%. 0.039 is the error rate, not the accuracy. The slide warns to quote the baseline, because most tokens are O and 0.602 comes for free.

written.q: Take the sentence 'the train slowly left the station'. Explain step by step how Lecture 6's parameter-free self-attention produces a contextual vector for 'station'. Why are dot products used, why is a softmax needed, and what happens if you scramble the words without positional information? How is that fixed?
written.m: Each token first gets a stand-alone vector from the embedding lookup table; none of these vectors knows about the others. For station (token i) we take the dot product with every token j, including itself. With unit-length vectors the dot product measures only the angle, so related words such as train score high (0.96) and the scores low (0.30). The scores cannot be weights yet because they can be negative and need not sum to 1, so we apply a softmax over j to get weights $w_{ij}$ that are positive and sum to one. The contextual vector is $\hat{x}_i = \sum_j w_{ij} x_j$: every vector is scaled by its weight and the results are added cell by cell, giving a vector the same size as the inputs that now contains information about train. Doing this for every token gives six vectors in and six out, with no trainable parameters. A weighted average ignores order, so 'the station left the train' gives identical vectors token for token. The fix is to add a vector that depends only on position (sine waves or learned) to each embedding before attention, so the same word at different positions enters attention as a different vector.
k: Embedding lookup gives stand-alone vectors that know nothing of their context
Dot products measure relatedness (the angle, for unit vectors)
Softmax makes the weights non-negative and sum to one
Contextual vector = weighted sum $\sum_j w_{ij} x_j$, same size as the inputs
Same computation for every token; no trainable parameters in L6
Scramble test: order-invariant, so identical vectors
Fix: add position vectors (sine or learned) to the embeddings

written.q: You must tag every token of airline queries with one of 123 slot labels. Describe a Transformer-encoder model from token IDs to predictions, giving tensor shapes for batch size B, sequence length L and d = 128. State what changes in the training loop compared with the Fashion-MNIST classifier, and explain how you would judge whether 0.961 token accuracy is good.
written.m: Input: token IDs of shape (B, L), padded with 0. Step 1: nn.Embedding(V, 128) gives (B, L, 128). Step 2: add learned position vectors from nn.Embedding(MAXLEN, 128) evaluated at arange(L), still (B, L, 128). Step 3: one nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(128, 4 heads, feed-forward width 4·128 = 512, batch_first=True) with src_key_padding_mask = (x == 0). It applies multi-head self-attention and then the same feed-forward MLP to each token, returning contextual vectors of shape (B, L, 128). Step 4: nn.Linear(128, 123) gives scores of shape (B, L, 123), and transpose(1, 2) turns them into (B, 123, L), the layout F.cross_entropy expects with targets of shape (B, L). Prediction is the argmax over the 123 classes for each token. Only the model line changes in the training loop: Adam, the DataLoader, cross_entropy, zero_grad, backward and step are untouched, and cross-entropy now runs over 123 classes per token. To judge 0.961, compare it with the majority-class baseline: always predicting O scores 0.602 because most tokens are O. The model gets 357 of 9,198 tokens wrong, cutting the error rate from about 39.8% to 3.9%. You can also inspect the attention weights, e.g. boston → from 0.47 and denver → to 0.38, to see whether the model uses sensible context.
k: Embedding + position embedding gives (B, L, d)
TransformerEncoderLayer: multi-head attention plus a per-token FFN (4d), with a padding mask
Per-token Linear(d, 123) and transpose to (B, 123, L) for cross_entropy
Training loop unchanged except building the model
Compare with the always-O baseline of 0.602; error 39.8% → 3.9%
Use the attention weights as a sanity check
